chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Jonah Jones in Horace's band and the Fletcher band kidding tradition
summary: Jonah Jones, a Louisville sight reader, joined Horace's first tour around Buffalo and Erie, brought Russell Bowles along, then joined Fletcher where he picked up the band's habit of kidding.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Well, following our line of names here, another person I have on the list here is Jonah Jones.

I always try to think if he was given a nickname. I can't recall, because if you've ever played in Fletcher's band, they always give you a name. Somebody gives you a nickname. Whether you like it or not, you accept it eventually. I can't think what Jonah was called, but nevertheless Jonah is originally from Louisville, Kentucky, and he wasn't in my Wilberforce band, but he joined me when I was going to make a tour, my first tour, and he was always an excellent reader. He could play first, second or third, and he was a sight reader, great -- and we went to Buffalo, New York, and played quite a few dates around Buffalo, New York, and Erie, Pennsylvania.

And we traveled quite a bit. I had a cousin of his named Russell Bowles, a trombone player that was one of the section men in the great Jimmie Lunceford band, and Russell was related to him, Jonah Jones, and Jonah got him in the

band with me because he knew quite a few guys in Louisville who wanted to get away, you know, and travel and get experience. So he helped me get quite a few guys out of there and, of course, we played Cincinnati, Ohio, too. There was a bandleader in Cincinnati, Ohio, named Wes Helvey, and Jonah did quite a stick with Wes Helvey's band.

And he always liked to play. He came to play, and he was a nice guy. And he -- later on, in later years, played in Fletcher's band. He was in that great band with Chu Berry and Hawk and those guys. And Jonah got to be quite a kidder too, like the other guys. In fact if you joined during the era that Fletcher's band, usually Earl and Buster Bailey and Red Allen and Coleman Hawkins, if you weren't a kidder, you either accepted it or you weren't in there long.

But Jonah did, and he talked -- they were funny. So a lot of that rubbed off on you, you know, and right now if you talk to Jonah -- I haven't seen Jonah since I played in Las Vegas and he had his group there. They had a great little 4-piece group but we got to talking over these times that I'm talking about now, and he injected quite a bit of the humor that existed during that time, the backtalk and the way he described things sounded just like Hawk and those guys. I said, 'I still see you carrying on the tradition of the old Fletcher Henderson band with this, you know, the giving guys
a bad time in a nice way, you know.

He said, 'Well, man, this is where it is, you know. And I'm looking forward One of those things -- but he's a great guy. (Inaudible) to seeing him, because I've been reading a little about him, thank god, he's still alive.
